title: Colliding galaxies make love, not war
caption: The Antennae galaxies, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Antennae Galaxies, NGC4038, NGC4039 · constellation Corvus · about 75 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: Credit: NASA, ESA, and the Hubble Heritage Team (STScI/AURA)-ESA/Hubble Collaboration. Acknowledgement: B. Whitmore ( Space Telescope Science Institute) and James Long (ESA/Hubble).

recognition.text: Official ESA/Hubble press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: This Hubble image shows the Antennae galaxies, a pair of galaxies caught in the middle of merging. ESA describes it as the sharpest image yet of this colliding pair.

As the two galaxies smash into each other, the collision is triggering the birth of billions of stars. Most of them form in groups and clusters rather than on their own. The brightest and most compact of these groups are known as super star clusters.

Collisions between galaxies are rarely about individual stars crashing into one another, since the space between stars is vast. Instead, the huge clouds of gas in each galaxy are squeezed and compressed as they meet, and that compression can set off bursts of star formation. The Antennae show this process in action, which makes them a natural target for studying how such mergers build new stars.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (3.27 x 3.25 arcminutes) and distance (75 million light years), the frame spans roughly 71,000 × 71,000 light-years. Its light set out about 75 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and combines visible and near-infrared filters, plus a filter that isolates glowing hydrogen. The color assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: Part of this image uses near-infrared light, which is invisible to the eye, and the galaxies are far too faint to see in this detail without a large telescope.

explore: The Antennae lie about 75 million light-years away in the constellation Corvus. The brightest and most compact of the star groups born in their collision are the super star clusters, and this sharp Hubble view helps pick them out.
